title: Your first campaign
summary: Take a first campaign from empty account to first decisions: safe setup, a test budget you can afford, a simple structure built click by click in Ads Manager, a launch checklist and the kill, hold, keep and scale starting rules. This is where everything from the earlier modules gets used with real money, so it is built to keep mistakes small.

lessons.title: Set up your accounts the right way
objectives: By the end you can list every account and asset a first campaign needs.
By the end you can set up a profile, business account, ad account and payment method that stay healthy.
By the end you can confirm your offer approval, tracking link and any required ad authorization before you spend.

steps.p: A first campaign fails more often from a broken setup than from a bad ad. A declined card, a missing pixel or an offer you were never approved for can waste days. This lesson walks through every account and asset you need, in order, so launch day is calm.

d.s: Every shortcut here costs you later

steps.say: Here's something that surprises most beginners. A first campaign fails more often from a broken setup than from a bad ad. A declined card, a missing pixel, or an offer you were never approved for can waste days. So in this lesson we walk through every account and asset you need, in order. Set it up once, properly, because every shortcut here costs you later.

steps.p: Think of your setup as five pieces, each with one job. If any piece is missing or broken, the whole campaign stalls. Check all five before you plan a single ad or spend a single dollar.
steps.more: On Meta the business account is, at the time of writing, called a business portfolio and is managed through Meta Business Suite or Business Manager. Names change; check the current Ads Manager and the Meta help centre. TikTok, Snapchat and Google have the same pieces under different names: a business centre or manager account, one or more ad accounts, a profile or page, billing and a pixel or tag.

Ad account|where campaigns and spend live
Page|the public face your ads run from
Payment method|how the platform charges you
Tracking|pixel or dataset plus your offer link
steps.say: Think of your setup as five pieces, each with one job. Look at the cards. The business account holds your assets in one place. The ad account is where campaigns and spend live. The page is the public face your ads run from. The payment method is how the platform charges you. And tracking means your pixel or dataset plus your offer link. If any one piece is missing or broken, the whole campaign stalls, so check all five before you spend a single dollar.

steps.p: Do things in this order. Each step depends on the one before it. Doing them out of order is the most common reason beginners get stuck in review, see payment errors or lose access to their own assets.
steps.say: Now the order. Follow the arrows on screen. First, secure your profile. Then create the business account. Then add your page and ad account, add a payment method, install tracking, and finally get your offer link. Each step depends on the one before it. Doing them out of order is the most common reason beginners get stuck in review, hit payment errors, or lose access to their own assets.

steps.p: Your business assets are attached to your real personal profile. If that profile is hacked or restricted, everything attached to it can go too. Use your real name and details, and lock the profile down before you build anything on top of it.
steps.more: Platforms require real identities. Two-factor authentication (2FA) means a second code, usually from an authenticator app, is needed every time someone logs in from a new device. It stops most account takeovers, which often start with a fake 'copyright warning' message or a fake login page. If a teammate needs access, add them with their own profile and the smallest role that does the job. If you are ever restricted, follow the Ad account bans module.
d: Recovery email and phone up to date
Nobody else logs in as you
steps.say: Start with your personal profile, because your business assets are attached to it. If it's hacked or restricted, everything attached can go too. So use your real name and details. Turn on two factor authentication, which asks for a second code when someone logs in from a new device. Use a strong, unique password, keep your recovery email and phone up to date, and never let anyone else log in as you. If a teammate needs access, add them with their own profile.

steps.p: You will see people selling old ad accounts, rented profiles and 'agency accounts' that promise no limits. These break platform rules, get shut down without warning and can take your money with them. Build your own accounts slowly and honestly.

It's slower at the start, but it's the only foundation that lasts.

steps.p: The platform charges you as you spend. A card that declines halfway through a test pauses your ads and wastes the data you were building. Pick a payment method that works reliably for foreign currency charges and is in your own name.
steps.more: In many African markets, local bank cards have monthly limits on foreign currency spending, and those limits change. Ask your bank for your current limit before you launch. The ad account's currency and time zone are usually hard or impossible to change after you create the account, so choose them on purpose. An account spending limit is a total cap you set yourself; when it is reached, ads stop. Names change; check the current Ads Manager billing settings.

steps.say: Next, payment. The platform charges you as you spend, and a card that declines halfway through a test pauses your ads and wastes the data you were building. Go down the table. Make sure your card allows foreign charges, since many ad accounts bill in U S dollars. Know your monthly limit, because in many African markets local cards have foreign spending limits that change. Use a card in your own name, choose the account currency carefully, and set an account spending limit as a cap on costly mistakes.

steps.p: Example: your bank allows $200 a month in foreign card spending and your plan is 3 ad sets at $18, so $54 a day. The card will decline on day four, in the middle of your test. Find this out before launch, not after.

d.label: until a $200 limit runs out at $54 a day
d.note: Example. $200 ÷ $54 = 3.7, so the decline lands on day 4.

steps.say: Here's an example of why the card limit matters. Say your bank allows two hundred dollars a month in foreign card spending, and your plan is three ad sets at eighteen dollars, so fifty four dollars a day. Two hundred divided by fifty four is about three point seven days. That means the card declines on day four, right in the middle of your test. Find this out before launch, not after.

steps.h: Tracking you need on day one
steps.p: You cannot judge a campaign you cannot measure. At minimum you need the platform's pixel or dataset on your landing page and your tracked offer link from the network, with sub IDs that tell you which ad sent each conversion.
steps.more: The Tracking basics module explained these; full setup, click by click: Tracking setup lab module. For a first campaign keep it simple: one pixel or dataset, one standard event that matches your goal, and a tracking link with sub IDs filled with your campaign, ad set and ad names. At the time of writing, Meta lists the pixel under datasets in Events Manager. Names change; check the current Events Manager.

The network tracking link credits you for each action. Sub I Ds or U T M parameters show which ad brought the action. And a test conversion proves the whole chain works. For a first campaign, keep it simple: one pixel, one standard event that matches your goal, and sub I Ds filled with your campaign, ad set and ad names.

steps.say: Before you spend, confirm with your affiliate manager that you're approved and that your plan is allowed. Many offers restrict traffic sources, countries or wording, and conversions from traffic the offer doesn't allow are often not paid at all. So work through this checklist: approval in writing, your traffic source allowed, your geos and caps confirmed, the payout and hold period noted, and the creative and wording rules saved.

lessons.title: Plan a test budget you can afford
objectives: By the end you can work out break-even CPA and a target CPA from a payout.
By the end you can set a zero-conversion kill line and calculate a total test budget.
By the end you can turn a test budget into daily budgets and check that it is realistic.

steps.h: A test budget is a planned loss limit
steps.p: Your first campaign is an experiment. A test budget is the most you will spend to get an answer, decided before launch. It is money you accept may not come back. Planning it in advance stops you from making emotional decisions at midnight.

d.s: Not while you watch the numbers move

steps.say: Your first campaign is an experiment. A test budget is the most you'll spend to get an answer, decided before launch. It's money you accept may not come back. Why plan it in advance? Because deciding the limit before launch stops you making emotional decisions at midnight, while you watch the numbers move. Decide calmly now, and follow the plan later.

steps.p: Your test budget must be money that would not hurt you if it disappeared. No rent, school fees, loans or savings meant for something else. If the full budget would hurt, test smaller or wait. Paid traffic has no guaranteed return.

d.text: Never test with borrowed money or money you need for living costs. A test can lose all of its budget.

steps.say: Your test budget must be money that wouldn't hurt you if it disappeared. That means no rent, no school fees, no loans, and no savings meant for something else. If the full budget would hurt, test smaller or wait. Paid traffic has no guaranteed return. Read the warning on screen: never test with borrowed money or money you need for living costs, because a test can lose all of its budget.

steps.p: On a CPA offer, the payout is your break-even cost per action. If one conversion costs you more than the payout, you lose money on it. Every number in your budget plan starts from this one.
steps.more: Example: the network pays $30 per FTD (first-time deposit). If one FTD costs you $30 in ads, you broke even. At $25 you made $5. At $40 you lost $10. RevShare offers are harder to plan because their value arrives over months. For a first test, a fixed CPA offer is simpler to measure and judge.
steps.say: Every budget plan starts from one number, the payout. On a C P A offer, that's cost per acquisition, the payout is your break-even cost per action. Look at the equation: payout per action equals break-even C P A. For example, if the network pays thirty dollars per F T D, first-time deposit, and one F T D costs you thirty dollars in ads, you broke even. At twenty five you made five. At forty you lost ten. For a first test, a fixed C P A offer is simpler to measure than RevShare.

steps.p: Break-even is the ceiling. Your goal sits below it. A target CPA sits below the payout and leaves room for profit and for conversions the network may later reject. Pick your target before launch, then judge every result against it.
steps.more: Example: payout $30 and you want a 20% margin. $30 × 0.8 = $24 target CPA. The margin is your choice; the Budget and kill rules module uses 25% in its examples and many beginners start between 20% and 30%. Remember rejections too: if the network later rejects some FTDs as low quality, your real cost per paid FTD is higher than the dashboard showed on the day.
steps.say: Break-even is the ceiling. Your goal sits below it. That's your target C P A, which leaves room for profit and for conversions the network may later reject. The equation is payout times one minus your margin. Example: payout thirty dollars, and you want a twenty percent margin. Thirty times zero point eight is twenty four dollars. The margin is your choice; many beginners start between twenty and thirty percent. Pick your target before launch, then judge every result against it.

steps.p: Try it. Enter the payout and the margin you want to keep, then check your answer. The lead-to-deposit rate does not change the target CPA. Change the margin afterwards and watch how fast the target moves.

d.task: Payout $30 per FTD, margin 20%. What is your target CPA (max cost per FTD)?

steps.say: Now try it yourself. In this lab, you have a payout of thirty dollars per F T D and a margin of twenty percent. Your task is to work out the target C P A, the maximum you can pay per F T D. Note that the lead to deposit rate doesn't change the target. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Afterwards, change the margin and watch how fast the target moves.

steps.p: The zero-conversion kill line is how much one ad set may spend with 0 network-confirmed conversions before you switch it off. The starting rule is 2 × target CPA. Write it down before launch. Full rule card: Budget and kill rules module.

d.text: Example: target $24. Kill line 2 × $24 = $48. If an ad set spends $48 with 0 FTDs, switch it off. Starting rules; adapt to your vertical and data.

steps.say: Next, the zero-conversion kill line. That's how much one ad set may spend with zero network-confirmed conversions before you switch it off. The starting rule is two times your target C P A. Example: target twenty four dollars, so the kill line is forty eight. If an ad set spends forty eight dollars with zero F T Ds, switch it off. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your vertical and data, and write yours down before launch.

steps.p: Plan 2 to 3 × target CPA of spend for each ad set. 2 × lets the zero-conversion kill line work. 3 × lets you judge CPA on an ad set that does convert. Multiply by the number of ad sets and add a small buffer for overspend.
steps.say: How much should the whole test cost? Plan two to three times your target C P A of spend for each ad set. Two times lets the zero-conversion kill line work. Three times lets you judge C P A on an ad set that does convert. Look at the equation: number of ad sets, times three times target C P A, gives your test budget. Then add a small buffer for overspend.

steps.p: Example: target $24, so 3 × target is $72 per ad set. Three ad sets can cost up to 3 × $72 = $216 before every ad set has had a fair chance. Add about 10% for overspend and plan for roughly $240 in total.
steps.say: Let's put it together. This is an example. With a twenty four dollar target, three times target is seventy two dollars per ad set. Three ad sets can cost up to two hundred and sixteen dollars before every ad set has had a fair chance. That's the big number on screen. Add about ten percent for overspend, and you plan for roughly two hundred and forty dollars in total.

steps.p: Spread each ad set's $72 over a few days so the platform has time to deliver and you do not judge on one bad morning. Smaller daily budgets give slower answers. Bigger daily budgets give faster but noisier answers.
steps.more: Example figures for a $72 test budget per ad set. Spending it all in one day gives the platform little time to find the right people and leaves you judging on a small, noisy sample. Many beginners choose 3 to 5 days per ad set. The $18 row is the plan used in the rest of this module.
steps.say: Now spread each ad set's seventy two dollars over a few days, so the platform has time to deliver and you don't judge on one bad morning. Read the table. At twelve dollars a day it takes six days. At eighteen dollars, four days, and fifty four dollars a day across three ad sets. At thirty six dollars, just two days. Smaller daily budgets give slower answers; bigger ones give faster but noisier answers. The eighteen dollar row is the plan used through the rest of this module.

steps.h: Lab: daily budget per ad set
steps.p: Turn the plan into a daily number. You want room for 3 target CPAs of $24 in each ad set, spread over 4 days. Work it out, then check. Change the days afterwards to see the trade-off between speed and noise.

d.task: Room for 3 FTDs at a $24 target CPA over 4 days. What daily budget per ad set?

steps.say: Time for another lab. You want room for three target C P As of twenty four dollars in each ad set, spread over four days. Your task is to work out the daily budget per ad set. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Afterwards, change the number of days and notice the trade-off between speed and noise.

steps.p: Ad platforms learn who converts by watching conversions. At the time of writing, Meta says an ad set usually needs around 50 optimisation events in a week to leave the learning phase. A small test will not reach that with deposits, and that is fine for a first test.
steps.more: We are not certain the 50-events figure is still current; check the current help centre. What it means for you: early results bounce around, so you judge on the money rules you wrote, never on a single day. School 2 covers choosing an optimisation event that suits a small budget.

d.b: Judge on rules, not one day

steps.say: Here's an important reality. Ad platforms learn who converts by watching conversions. At the time of writing, Meta says an ad set usually needs around fifty optimisation events in a week to leave the learning phase. We're not certain that figure is still current, so check the help centre. A small test won't reach that with deposits, and that's fine. It just means early results bounce around, so you judge on the money rules you wrote, never on a single day.

steps.p: Work backwards to see whether one ad set's test budget can even buy a result. Example: $72 at $0.12 per click buys 600 clicks. If the funnel gives about 3 FTDs from that, the test is fair. If it gives 0.3, it is not.
steps.more: Example: CPC $0.12, so $72 ÷ $0.12 = 600 clicks. If 10% sign up, that is 60 sign-ups. If 5% of sign-ups deposit, that is 3 FTDs, a cost of $24 each, exactly on target. These rates are illustrations; real rates vary widely by geo, offer and funnel. If your honest estimate gives less than 1 FTD per ad set's test budget, pick a cheaper source or an offer with an easier conversion.
steps.say: Is your budget even realistic? Work backwards down this funnel. Example: seventy two dollars at twelve cents a click buys six hundred clicks. If ten percent sign up, that's sixty sign-ups. If five percent of those deposit, that's three F T Ds at twenty four dollars each, right on target. These rates are illustrations and real rates vary widely. If your honest estimate gives less than one F T D per ad set's budget, pick a cheaper source or an offer with an easier conversion.

steps.p: Most budget mistakes come from spreading money too thin or changing the plan mid-test. Example: $5 a day across 10 ad sets is $50 a day, yet each ad set needs more than 14 days to reach a $72 test budget.

lessons.title: Simple structure, honest creatives
objectives: By the end you can build a simple campaign structure that tests one variable.
By the end you can name campaigns, ad sets and ads so results are easy to read.
By the end you can write a basic, honest ad with a hook, body and call to action.

steps.p: Your first campaign should be easy to read. If you change ten things at once and it works, you will not know why. If it fails, you will not know what to fix. A simple structure turns every result into a lesson.

d.b: One campaign, a few ad sets, a few ads
d.s: Change one thing at a time

steps.say: Simple beats clever. Your first campaign should be easy to read. If you change ten things at once and it works, you won't know why. If it fails, you won't know what to fix. So the plan is one campaign, a few ad sets, and a few ads, changing only one thing at a time. That's how every result becomes a lesson.

steps.p: Most ad platforms use three levels. The campaign holds the goal. The ad set holds who sees the ads, where they appear and the budget. The ad is the creative and text that people actually see in their feed.

At twenty four hours, look at C T R, C P C, page views and sign-ups, and only use the zero F T D kill. steps.p: Before conversions arrive, a few early signals tell you whether the ad and page work at all. They are hints, not verdicts. Compare them with your other ads, because outside benchmarks vary by geo and vertical.
steps.more: If clicks are high but landing page views are much lower, people are leaving before the page loads, which is often a speed or link problem. Fix that at once. If one ad's CTR is far below your other ads, its hook may not be working. These are signals to investigate, not reasons to kill on day one.
d: Spend|is the ad delivering at all?
Clicks vs page views|is the page loading?
steps.say: Before conversions arrive, a few early signals tell you whether the ad and page work at all. Spend: is the ad delivering? C T R, click-through rate: are people stopping to click? C P C, cost per click: what does each click cost? And clicks versus page views: is the page loading? If clicks are high but page views much lower, people leave before the page loads, so fix that at once. These are hints to investigate, not reasons to kill on day one.

steps.p: Most platforms put an ad set back into learning after significant edits, which resets the data it has gathered. In the first 72 hours, make only the changes your rules require, and fix anything broken at once.
steps.more: What counts as a significant edit differs by platform and changes over time. Check the current help centre. When in doubt, wait for your next checkpoint.

b.title: Fine in the first 72 hours
items: Pausing an ad set at its kill line

steps.say: Most platforms put an ad set back into learning after significant edits, which resets the data it has gathered. Compare the columns. Changing the creative, big budget jumps, or changing the audience or conversion event can reset learning. But fixing a broken link, always, pausing an ad set at its kill line, and logging numbers in your sheet are fine. What counts as significant varies and changes, so check the help centre, and when in doubt, wait for your next checkpoint.

steps.p: At each checkpoint, run every ad set through the same questions in the same order. The first yes decides. Write the answer in your sheet. This turns a stressful moment into a two-minute routine you can repeat for years.
d: Spend ≥ 3 × target, CPA over kill line? Kill
steps.say: At each checkpoint, run every ad set through the same questions, in the same order. The first yes decides. Zero F T Ds at two times target? Kill. Spend at three times target with C P A over the kill line? Kill. Three or more F T Ds with C P A at or below zero point eight times target? Scale. Three or more F T Ds at or below target? Keep. Anything else? Hold. Write the answer in your sheet. It becomes a two minute routine.

steps.more: The CPA kill line is the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even: 1.5 × $24 = $36, but break-even is $30, so the line is $30. It only applies once spend reaches 3 × target, $72, because before that one FTD more or less swings the CPA too much. Three conversions is a bare minimum before you trust a CPA. Scale means +20%, with at least 48 hours between steps. Keep means it works at target: leave the budget alone.

steps.p: Example: at 72 hours ad set B has spent $54 and brought 3 network-confirmed FTDs. That is a CPA of $18, at or under the $19.20 scale line (0.8 × $24). Decision: scale, with a budget increase of 20%.

steps.say: Ad set B, also an example. At seventy two hours it has spent fifty four dollars and brought three network-confirmed F T Ds. So the decision is scale, with a budget increase of twenty percent.

steps.p: Example: ad set C has spent $54 and brought 1 FTD, a CPA of $54. That looks terrible, but spend is still under 3 × target ($72) and there is only 1 conversion, so neither kill row is true yet. Decision: hold.

steps.more: Why not kill now? One FTD more by $72 would make the CPA $36, and two more $24. Below 3 × target, single conversions swing the CPA too much to judge. If C reaches $72 with still only 1 FTD, its CPA is $72, above the $30 kill line, and it is killed then.

One more F T D by seventy two dollars would make the C P A thirty six, two more would make it twenty four. If C reaches seventy two with still only one, it's killed then.

steps.p: Scaling means spending more on what works. On a first test, scale slowly and keep watching CPA. A winner at $18 a day is not guaranteed to win at $180 a day, because new spend reaches new, often colder, people.

quiz.q: Payout $30, target CPA $24. After 72 hours an ad set spent $69 and brought 3 network-confirmed FTDs. What do you do?
options: Kill it
Scale +20%
Keep it: no budget change
Change the creative

options: Keep it because the CTR is high
Kill it, because the rule is about paid results
Double the budget
Change the audience and keep going
quiz.why: 2 × $25 = $50 with 0 network-confirmed FTDs. CTR is a hint; the kill rule is about the result you are paid for.

quiz.q: Why not double the budget on a winner on day 2?
options: Big jumps can disrupt delivery and early data is noisy
Platforms do not allow it
It lowers the network payout
It always stops the ad

Hold it
Scale it
Delete the campaign

quiz.q: An ad has 200 clicks but only 70 landing page views. What is the most likely issue?

The payout is too low
The audience is too broad
The page loads slowly or the link is broken

options: Keep it running for one more day
Kill it: it reached the zero-conversion kill line of 2 × target
Raise the budget so it finds buyers faster
Change the creative and keep the same ad set

options: The card declines during day 3, mid-test
Nothing, $200 covers a week
The card declines on day 8
The platform lowers your budget automatically

exam.q: You want to learn which of three angles works best in Nigeria. Which structure is best?
options: Three ad sets in three different countries
One ad set with 15 ads of mixed angles and formats
Three ad sets, same audience and budget, one angle each
Three campaigns with different conversion events
exam.why: Keeping everything else the same makes the angle the only variable, so the result answers your question.

Run it from a new ad account
Send reviewers to a harmless page
Pause, apply for the required authorization and check local law before running

exam.q: Payout $30, target $24. At 72 hours an ad set spent $45 and brought 3 FTDs. What is the CPA and the decision?

$15 CPA, double the budget today

Check it is delivering and the link works, then wait for your checkpoint
Move its budget to the others
exam.why: Early numbers are noisy. In the first hours you only check that things work, then judge at planned checkpoints.

exam.q: Ads Manager shows 12 conversions but your network shows 0 sign-ups from 500 clicks. What is the first thing to check?
options: The ad's CTR
The offer link, sub IDs and a fresh test conversion
The audience size
The ad copy for spelling
exam.why: When two systems disagree this much, the tracking chain is the likely cause. Re-test the link and conversion first.

exam.q: Payout $30, target $24. An ad set spent $80 and brought 2 network-confirmed FTDs. What does the rule card say?
options: Hold, fewer than 3 FTDs
Scale, it has conversions
Kill: spend is past 3 × target ($72) and the $40 CPA is over the $30 kill line
Keep, CPA is close to target
exam.why: The kill line is the lower of 1.5 × $24 = $36 and break-even $30, so $30. Spend $80 ≥ $72 and CPA $40 > $30, so kill.

exam.q: An ad set has a CPA of $18 against a $24 target at $20 a day, with 4 network FTDs over 3 days. What is a sensible next step?
options: Raise it to $200 a day
Raise it to $24 a day and wait at least 48 hours before another step
Pause it to protect the profit
Change the audience to find more people
exam.why: $18 is under the $19.20 scale line with 3+ FTDs. A 20% step ($20 to $24), then at least 48 hours, keeps delivery stable.
